snip.t: Respiratory signs – cough, hemoptysis, dyspnoea, sinusitis, otitis media: Pulmonary capillaritis (hemoptysis) is typical of ANCA vasculitis; chronic sinusitis points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Congenital and genetic: Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener: bronchiectasis, sinusitis, dextrocardia), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Young's syndrome

Signs: finger clubbing, coarse crackles (often early to mid-inspiratory and moving with cough), wheeze, rhonchi; signs of cause (sinusitis, dextrocardia, joint disease); in advanced disease cyanosis and cor pulmonale.
Predisposing factors: Establish HIV status, ART history, prior tuberculosis or contact, sickle cell disease, recent otitis media, sinusitis, or base of skull trauma (rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea).
HEENT: *Conjunctival injection, oropharyngeal erythema, tonsillar exudate, sinus tenderness?* — Upper respiratory sources; sinusitis can seed lower tract.
Recurrent infections (sinusitis, pneumonia, skin): Immunoparesis from suppressed normal immunoglobulins; also common in HIV‑positive patients.
Head: Scalp tenderness, sinus tenderness, temporal artery thickening — Temporal arteritis (elderly); sinusitis; meningitis (neck stiffness)
Mechanical: tube malposition (into the airway), blockage, sinusitis, nasal erosion and ulceration, tube displacement, pressure necrosis, leakage around a gastrostomy.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic sinusitis, hemoptysis, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Serologic testing demonstrates strong positivity for c-ANCA. Which condition is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis classically features c-ANCA positivity along with upper and lower respiratory tract lesions and glomerulonephritis. Microscopic polyangiitis typically presents with p-ANCA rather than c-ANCA.
qs.s: Cardiovascular & Respiratory Pathology: Atherosclerosis, RHD & MI: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man has a 3-month history of recurrent sinusitis, epistaxis, haemoptysis, and haematuria. CXR shows bilateral cavitating nodules. Urinalysis shows red cell casts. c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) is strongly positive. Most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: This is a classic presentation of Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA), formerly Wegener's granulomatosis. It is a small vessel vasculitis characterized by necrotizing granulomas involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts, glomerulonephritis, and is strongly associated with c-ANCA (antibodies against proteinase 3, PR3-ANCA).

qs.q: Which statement about phaeohyphomycosis is correct? Dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi causing phaeohyphomycosis can produce a spectrum from localized sinusitis to subcutaneous cysts to disseminated disease. ---
o: Infection only occurs in immunocompetent patients
Cases rarely respond to treatment with oral itraconazole
Infected tissue reveals branching septate nonpigmented hyphae
Phaeohyphomycosis may exhibit subcutaneous or systemic disease
Causative agents are normal flora easily isolated from skin
qs.e: Phaeohyphomycosis encompasses a broad clinical spectrum ranging from localized subcutaneous cysts to disseminated systemic disease and sinusitis.

qs.q: Which statement regarding aspergillosis is correct? Aspergillus causes a wide range of local infections (otomycosis, keratitis, onychomycosis, sinusitis) beyond invasive pulmonary disease; blood cultures are usually negative even in invasive disease, so c is false. ---
o: Clinical manifestations include local infections of the ear and sinuses
Bone marrow transplant recipients are not at risk for invasive disease
Patients on parenteral corticosteroids are not at risk for invasive disease
Pulmonary aspergillosis is frequently diagnosed by culturing blood samples
Patients with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis rarely have eosinophilia
qs.e: Aspergillus species frequently cause localized infections involving the ear, cornea, nails, and sinuses in addition to pulmonary manifestations.

qs.q: Two brothers have recurrent pneumonia, meningitis, sinusitis, and infections with Pneumocystis and Giardia. IgG 47, IgA 5, IgM 671 mg/dL. Normal B and T cells. Most likely gene mutation?
qs.e: Very high IgM + very low IgG and IgA = hyper-IgM syndrome. CD40L mutation prevents CD40-CD40L interaction needed for isotype switching from IgM to other classes.

es.q: A patient presents with chronic sinusitis, hemoptysis, and a characteristic nasal perforation. Lab tests reveal the presence of ANCA. What specific ANCA subtype is most commonly associated with this condition? → c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) in Wegener Granulomatosis.
es.m:
- **Specific marker**: Strongly linked to the presence of cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, specifically c-ANCA targeting proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA).
- **Syndrome identification**: The constellation of chronic sinusitis, hemoptysis, and nasal perforation points to Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener Granulomatosis).
- **Triad involvement**: Characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tracts coupled with renal glomerular disease.
- **Histological hallmarks**: Biopsy reveals vasculitis, necrosis, and granulomas involving small-to-medium-sized vessels.
- **Diagnostic utility**: High specificity of c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) assists in ea

ai.title: Sinusitis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses, usually infectious. Diagnosis relies on history, exam and simple imaging. Management focuses on treating infection, relieving pressure and preventing complications.

sections.p: Sinusitis is inflammation of the mucosa lining the paranasal sinuses. Acute disease lasts <4 weeks, subacute 4–12 weeks, chronic >12 weeks. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by plain‑film sinus X‑ray or CT if available.
b: History of facial pain, nasal discharge, fever, cough
Anterior rhinoscopy: purulent nasal discharge, mucosal edema
CT shows mucosal thickening or opacification

t.b: Shows sinus opacification or air‑fluid level – confirms sinus involvement when CT unavailable
Gold standard for chronic sinusitis, shows mucosal thickening, polyps, ostial obstruction

sections.p: Use the Lund‑Mackay score on CT for chronic disease; acute disease is staged by symptom duration and presence of systemic signs.
b: Acute uncomplicated – <4 weeks, mild fever, no systemic signs
Acute complicated – facial swelling, vision change, meningitis signs

t.b: Each sinus scored 0–2; total 0–24; >12 suggests severe chronic disease

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, viral upper respiratory infection is most common. Bacterial superinfection follows, often with Strep pyogenes or Staph aureus.
b: Bacterial superinfection (Strep pyogenes, Staph aureus, Haemophilus influenzae)

t.b: Identifies immunosuppression that predisposes to fungal or atypical bacterial sinusitis
Rule out pulmonary TB or pneumonia that may seed sinuses

sections.p: Patients report facial pain or pressure, nasal congestion, purulent discharge, post‑nasal drip, cough, and sometimes fever. Chronic cases have nasal obstruction and anosmia.

t.b: Shows mucosal edema, purulent discharge – confirms sinusitis

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on history, exam and plain X‑ray. CT is reserved for chronic or complicated cases.

t.b: Detects sinus opacification or air‑fluid level – confirms sinus involvement when CT unavailable
Gold standard for chronic sinusitis, shows mucosal thickening, polyps, ostial obstruction

sections.p: Urgent referral needed for facial swelling, vision changes, severe headache, fever >39 °C, or neurological signs. Complications include orbital cellulitis, meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Treat the underlying cause, relieve pressure, and monitor. First‑line antibiotics cover common bacteria; avoid macrolides if resistance high. Use decongestants and saline irrigation.

t.b: Covers Strep pyogenes, Staph aureus, H. influenzae – first‑line in uncomplicated acute sinusitis
Reserve for patients with penicillin allergy or treatment failure

sections.p: Re‑evaluate in 7–10 days; if symptoms persist, consider imaging. Prevent by treating allergic rhinitis, avoiding smoking, and ensuring good hand hygiene.

t.b: Identifies allergic triggers that worsen sinusitis

sections.p: Upper respiratory tract infection, dental abscess, migraine, temporal arteritis, and orbital cellulitis.
b: Dental abscess – pain localised to tooth, swelling of cheek

sections.p: Plain X‑ray may miss early sinusitis; normal white cell count can occur in viral cases. CT may over‑interpret mucosal thickening as disease.
b: CT mucosal thickening in allergic rhinitis

faq.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of acute sinusitis?
faq.a: Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus are most common in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: When should I order a CT scan?
faq.a: When symptoms persist >4 weeks, or if there are red flags like facial swelling or visual changes.

faq.q: Can I use a nasal steroid spray for acute sinusitis?
faq.a: No, steroids are reserved for chronic or allergic sinusitis; they do not help acute infection.

exam: What is the first line antibiotic for uncomplicated acute sinusitis? — Amoxicillin‑clavulanate; covers common bacteria, safe in pregnancy, low resistance in many settings.
Which red flag would prompt immediate imaging? — Facial swelling beyond sinus borders; indicates possible orbital cellulitis or abscess.
How would you differentiate sinusitis from a dental abscess on exam? — Dental abscess shows tooth pain and cheek swelling; sinusitis shows facial pain over sinus and purulent nasal discharge.
What is the rationale for using saline irrigation in sinusitis? — It mechanically clears mucus, reduces bacterial load, and improves mucociliary clearance.
When is a fluoroquinolone indicated in sinusitis? — Penicillin allergy or treatment failure after 5 days of first‑line therapy.
How would you manage a patient with chronic sinusitis who is HIV positive? — Treat infection, consider fungal causes, ensure ART adherence, and monitor for opportunistic infections.
What complication is most feared in untreated acute sinusitis? — Orbital cellulitis leading to vision loss.
Why is a CT scan preferred over plain X‑ray in chronic sinusitis? — CT provides detailed mucosal and ostial assessment, guiding surgical planning.
